Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-prompt-long-0119", "row_sha256": "ec37fa97b9b14e73cf39090199b0bb819c33af814ef64253037f65a82d42965a", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
lowercase rough request here, could you help me make a practical migration plan for our team’s shared documents moving from the old shared drive into the new workspace. i need the plan to be something the team can actually follow, not a broad essay about digital change. address it to Celeste, not Jasper. Celeste is coordinating the migration, and Jasper is not the recipient for this request. the plan should cover preparation, the move itself, and what we do after it, but it should not claim that the migration has already happened or assume a date we have not settled.

we have a mixture of working documents, reference material, and older files on the shared drive. the working documents include drafts that people still edit and files that have an owner but have not been opened recently. reference material includes policies and instructions that staff look up but do not usually edit. there are also old project folders, a few duplicate files, and some documents whose purpose is not obvious from the name. please make those differences matter in the plan. don’t treat every file as something to copy automatically, and don’t suggest that an unclear file should simply be deleted. the team needs a sensible way to identify what needs a decision before it moves.

for the prep part, ask for an inventory that is useful without making it sound like a new records system. include the current folder or file name, who owns it if we know, whether it is active or reference material, and any access or link issue that could affect the move. if an owner is unknown, mark that as unknown rather than guessing. mention that people should flag duplicates and files they cannot identify. i would like a short way to gather questions from staff too, since some people use links saved in their own notes and may not remember where the original document lives. don’t imply that everyone has to audit the whole drive on their own.

there is a naming issue we have to keep in view. some folders have team names that changed last year, while old links still use the previous names. the plan should say how we can map those older names to the current folder names, and say that the mapping needs to be checked by the relevant folder owner before it is treated as settled. we do not have a complete list of the changed names yet. please don’t fabricate a list or state that the owners have approved anything. if a folder has no clear owner, leave a way to record that for follow-up rather than assigning it to someone by default.

for the actual move, keep the sequence understandable: first decide what is ready, then move the agreed files, then check the result. include a limited trial with one team folder before the wider move, but don’t choose which folder for us. explain that the trial is for spotting practical issues such as permissions, broken links, and folder structure, not proof that every file will behave the same way. after the trial, the team should be able to adjust the steps before proceeding. where an access setting cannot be matched in the new workspace, the plan should tell the team to record the issue and ask the owner to decide, instead of silently widening access or blocking people without discussion.

we want to avoid two copies getting edited at once. please include a clear point at which people are told to stop editing the source copy while its agreed destination is being moved, and say how the team will tell people when editing can resume in the new workspace. keep that as a communication step, not a claim that we already have a date or a messaging channel. one person said, “I can’t tell which copy is current when both links still work.” that is the sort of practical concern the plan should address. don’t turn that quote into a claim that everyone has had the same problem.

please include a numbered section for the checks after a move. the checks should cover whether expected files arrived, whether the folder names and structure make sense, whether the right people can open and edit what they need, and whether key links still lead to the intended document. include a way to note anything missing or not working and send it to the relevant owner for follow-up. if a problem is found, the plan should distinguish fixing it from marking the whole migration complete; don’t say that a check has passed before anyone carries it out. keep the checks realistic for a team rather than promising a technical audit of every file.

also address old project folders and duplicate or unclear files in the after-move part. the team should be able to leave an item out of the move temporarily when its owner or purpose needs clarification, while recording where it was left and who needs to review it. don’t turn “temporarily left out” into “discarded,” and don’t assume that an old project folder has no continuing value. give us a clear way to record a decision once it is made, without inventing a retention rule or deciding the fate of any particular file.

please make the result a concise but usable team prompt for producing this migration plan, with enough detail that the writer knows what to cover and what not to assume. include preparation, trial, wider move, follow-up, and staff communication in a sensible order. the plan should be grounded in the details above and written in plain English. keep the final paragraph about the issue of saved links in staff notes and the questions we need to collect; that point matters separately from the file checks. don’t add a conclusion that says the team is ready to migrate, because we have not made that decision.", "output": "Create a practical, plain-English migration plan for our team’s shared documents, moving them from the old shared drive into the new workspace. Address the plan to Celeste, not Jasper. Celeste is coordinating the migration; Jasper is not the recipient. Make the plan usable by the team rather than a broad essay about digital change. Cover preparation, the move, and follow-up without claiming that the migration has happened or assuming an unsettled date.

Our shared drive contains working documents, reference material, older files, old project folders, duplicates, and documents whose purpose is unclear from their names. Working documents include drafts people still edit and files with an owner that have not been opened recently. Reference material includes policies and instructions that staff look up but do not usually edit. Reflect these differences in the plan. Do not treat every file as an automatic move, and do not recommend simply deleting files whose purpose is unclear. Explain how the team can identify items that need a decision before they move.

For preparation, propose a useful inventory without turning it into a new records system. Include the current folder or file name, the owner if known, whether the item is active or reference material, and any access or link issue that could affect the move. Mark an unknown owner as unknown rather than guessing. Include a way for people to flag duplicates and files they cannot identify. Provide a short way to collect staff questions, including questions about links saved in personal notes and uncertainty about where the original document lives. Do not imply that everyone must audit the entire drive individually.

Account for folder names that changed last year while old links still use the previous names. Describe how to map previous names to current folder names, and make clear that the relevant folder owner must check the mapping before it is treated as settled. We do not yet have a complete list of changed names, so do not invent one or state that owners have approved anything. If a folder has no clear owner, provide a way to record it for follow-up rather than assigning it to someone by default.

Use an understandable sequence for the move: decide what is ready, move the agreed files, and check the result. Include a limited trial using one team folder, but do not choose the folder for us. Explain that the trial is intended to identify practical issues such as permissions, broken links, and folder structure; it is not proof that every file will behave the same way. Allow the team to adjust the steps after the trial and before proceeding with the wider move. If an access setting cannot be matched in the new workspace, direct the team to record the issue and ask the owner to decide. Do not silently widen access or block people without discussion.

Address the risk of two copies being edited at once. Include a clear point when people are told to stop editing the source copy while its agreed destination is being moved, and explain how they will be told when editing can resume in the new workspace. Treat this as a communication step, not as a claim that a date or messaging channel has already been selected. One person said, “I can’t tell which copy is current when both links still work.” Address this kind of practical concern without suggesting that everyone has experienced the same problem.

Use a numbered section for post-move checks:
1. Check whether the expected files arrived.
2. Check whether folder names and structure make sense.
3. Check whether the right people can open and edit what they need.
4. Check whether key links still lead to the intended document.
5. Record anything missing or not working and send it to the relevant owner for follow-up.

Distinguish fixing a problem from marking the whole migration complete. Do not say a check has passed before someone carries it out, and do not promise a technical audit of every file. Keep the checks realistic for a team.

In the follow-up, cover old project folders, duplicates, and unclear files. Allow an item to be temporarily left out while its owner or purpose is clarified, while recording where it was left and who needs to review it. Do not describe a temporarily omitted item as discarded, assume an old project folder has no continuing value, invent a retention rule, or decide the fate of a particular file. Provide a clear way to record a decision once it is made.

Make the result a concise but usable prompt for a writer producing this migration plan, with enough detail to show what to cover and what not to assume. Present preparation, trial, wider move, follow-up, and staff communication in a sensible order. Ground the plan in the details above and use plain English. In the final paragraph, separately address staff questions about saved links in personal notes and where the original document lives; this is distinct from the file checks. Do not conclude that the team is ready to migrate, because that decision has not been made."}]
